original_value: Root and butt-rot (RBR) has a significant impact on both the material and economic outcome of timber harvesting, and therewith on the individual forest owner and collectively on the forest and wood processing industries. An accurate recording of the presence of RBR during timber harvesting would enable a mapping of the location and extent of the problem, providing a basis for evaluating spread in a climate anticipated to enhance pathogenic growth in the future. Therefore, a system to automatically identify and detect the presence of RBR would constitute an important contribution to addressing the problem without increasing workload complexity for the machine operator. In this study, we developed and evaluated an approach based on RGB images to automatically detect tree stumps and classify them as to the absence or presence of rot. Furthermore, since knowledge of the extent of RBR is valuable in categorizing logs, we also classify stumps into three classes of infestation; rot = 0%, 0% < rot < 50% and rot ≥ 50%. In this work we used deep-learning approaches and conventional machine-learning algorithms for detection and classification tasks. The results showed that tree stumps were detected with precision rate of 95% and recall of 80%. Using only the correct output (TP) of the stump detector, stumps without and with RBR were correctly classified with accuracy of 83.5% and 77.5%, respectively. Classifying rot into three classes resulted in 79.4%, 72.4%, and 74.1% accuracy for stumps with rot = 0%, 0% < rot < 50%, and rot ≥ 50%, respectively. With some modifications, the developed algorithm could be used either during the harvesting operation to detect RBR regions on the tree stumps or as an RBR detector for post-harvest assessment of tree stumps and logs.

result.paraphrase: Root and butt rot (RBR) has a major effect on both the material and economic results of timber harvesting, and thus on individual forest owners as well as the forest and wood-processing industries as a whole. Recording RBR accurately during harvesting would make it possible to map the problem’s location and extent, creating a basis for assessing its spread in a future climate expected to favor pathogenic growth. For this reason, an automatic system for identifying and detecting RBR would be an important step toward solving the problem without adding to the machine operator’s workload. In this study, we developed and assessed an RGB-image-based method to automatically detect tree stumps and classify them by whether rot is absent or present. In addition, because information on the degree of RBR is useful for log categorization, we also divided stumps into three infestation classes: rot = 0%, 0% < rot < 50%, and rot ≥ 50%. We used deep-learning methods together with conventional machine-learning algorithms for the detection and classification tasks. Tree stumps were detected with a precision of 95% and a recall of 80%. Using only the true positive output from the stump detector, stumps without and with RBR were classified correctly with accuracies of 83.5% and 77.5%, respectively. When rot was grouped into three classes, the accuracies were 79.4%, 72.4%, and 74.1% for stumps with rot = 0%, 0% < rot < 50%, and rot ≥ 50%, respectively. With some modifications, the algorithm could be used either during harvesting to identify RBR regions on tree stumps or after harvesting as an RBR detector for assessing tree stumps and logs.
